title: Constipation, pain medicines and frailty in arthritis (UK)

direct_answer: Some pain medicines, especially opioids such as codeine and morphine, commonly cause constipation. Frailty, less movement and lower fluid intake add to the risk. Fluids, fibre, movement and a laxative if advised can help. Talk to your pharmacist or GP before changing medicines.

content:
Constipation is uncomfortable and can affect appetite, mood and confusion in older people.

This guide covers prevention and help. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why it happens

  • Opioid pain medicines slow the gut.
  • Less movement.
  • Drinking and eating less.

Things you can try

  • Drink regularly.
  • Include fibre such as fruit, vegetables and wholegrains.
  • Move gently.
  • Use a footstool on the toilet.

Medicines

Ask your pharmacist or GP about a laxative if you take codeine or similar. Ask for a medicine review.

Constipation after an operation

  • Constipation is common after surgery such as joint replacement.
  • Ask the ward team or your pharmacist about a laxative if you go home on strong painkillers.
  • Drink regularly and move as advised.
  • Contact your GP or NHS 111 if you have not opened your bowels for several days, have tummy pain or swelling, or are being sick.

When to get help

  • Get urgent help if you have severe tummy pain, are being sick, or notice blood in your stool.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I stop my painkiller?

Do not stop without advice.

Can constipation cause confusion?

In older people it can contribute.

Sources and further reading
